title: Wooden posts and split boards rest 20 metres down in a German lake
dek: Archaeologists recovered worked wood up to 10,500 years old from Lake Arendsee. The pieces may belong to structures built by hunter-gatherers millennia before farming arrived.
body: Divers working for the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology of Saxony-Anhalt brought up a post roughly 1.6 metres tall with clear felling marks and split boards up to 1.3 metres long. The wood lay beneath about 20 metres of water in Lake Arendsee, in the Altmarkkreis Salzwedel district of northern Germany. Such preservation is rare for the Mesolithic, when stone tools and animal bones usually survive but timber almost never does.

State archaeologist Harald Meller said the finds shed a completely new light on a period known in Central Germany mainly from soil discolourations. Project manager Marcel Weiß noted that identifying the structures could change how archaeologists understand Mesolithic communities and the development of cultural landscapes. If the remains represent permanent or intensively used living areas, they would predate the first farming longhouses in Central Europe by around 3,000 years.

The lake's unusual geology made the survival possible. An underlying salt dome has caused the lake bottom to subside slowly, preserving parts of the ancient shoreline and archaeological material under a relatively thin sediment layer. Unlike many inland lakes where silting buries shorelines, this process kept the Mesolithic land surface accessible to modern investigation.

People were already known to have lived along the lake's shores during the Mesolithic. The region is also associated with the individual known as the Shaman of Bad Dürrenberg, whose grave has provided important evidence about Mesolithic life. The new wooden finds add a structural dimension to that picture.

After the initial discovery in spring 2026, a second investigation deployed a remotely operated vehicle from the Fraunhofer IOSB-AST in Ilmenau. High-resolution sonar mapped the submerged landscape and documented the former shoreline contours. By recording the precise position of each discovery, researchers hope to identify concentrations of material that could indicate archaeological sites and guide future underwater work.

Lake Arendsee has yielded finds from several periods in recent years, including Neolithic fish weirs, a High Medieval flat-bottomed cargo vessel and a Late Medieval dugout canoe. The latest discoveries push the lake's archaeological record considerably further back and could provide unusually direct evidence of how Mesolithic communities worked with wood.

Researchers are now attempting to establish whether the posts and boards formed part of huts, another type of construction or something not previously identified in the archaeological record. The answer could provide a rare glimpse of structures built by hunter-gatherers more than 10 millennia ago, structures that survived beneath Lake Arendsee while most comparable traces on land disappeared.
doesnt_show: The finds do not yet show what kind of structures the timbers formed, whether they represent permanent dwellings or seasonal camps, or how extensively the shoreline was occupied.
settle: Detailed spatial analysis of the timber positions combined with further radiocarbon dates and microstratigraphic work would clarify the nature and duration of the structures.
